notes.summary: Mixture questions ask what happens when two or more things with different prices, strengths or ratios are mixed. Most of them are solved with one idea: alligation, a quick way to handle a weighted average. SSC asks 0 to 1 question in Tier 1 and up to 2 in Tier 2, and alligation also speeds up profit, interest and average questions.

concepts.title: Weighted average: the mean price
concepts.body:
When quantities q₁ and q₂ with prices (or strengths) p₁ and p₂ are mixed, the mean price is

Mean = (q₁p₁ + q₂p₂)/(q₁ + q₂)

Example: 8 kg at ₹51 and 9 kg at ₹68. Mean = (408 + 612)/17 = 1020/17 = ₹60 per kg.

The mean always lies between the two prices and is closer to the price of the larger quantity.

concepts.title: The rule of alligation
concepts.body:
To find the ratio in which two kinds must be mixed to get a given mean:

Cheaper quantity : Dearer quantity = (Dearer − Mean) : (Mean − Cheaper)

Cheaper cDearer d
Mean m
d − mm − c

Example: rice at ₹20 and ₹25, mean ₹22. Ratio = (25 − 22) : (22 − 20) = 3 : 2.

Cross the differences: each kind gets the difference on the other side.

concepts.title: Water and pure liquid in alligation
concepts.body:
Water is free, so its price is ₹0. Pure milk has 100% milk; water has 0% milk.

Milk at ₹60 per litre made worth ₹50 by adding water: water : milk = (60 − 50) : (50 − 0) = 10 : 50 = 1 : 5.

For strengths: 80% and 90% acid mixed to make 87%: 80% part : 90% part = (90 − 87) : (87 − 80) = 3 : 7. In 20 litres, the 80% solution is 6 litres.

concepts.title: Alligation works for any average
concepts.body:
Alligation is just a fast way to handle a weighted average. Use it for:

  • Profit percent: part sold at 8% gain and part at 18% gain, overall 14%. Ratio = (18 − 14) : (14 − 8) = 2 : 3.
  • Interest rates: ₹10,000 lent partly at 8% and partly at 12% earns ₹1,000 a year, so the average rate is 10%; the parts are 1 : 1, ₹5,000 each.
  • Speeds: the average speed is a weighted average by time, so alligation gives the ratio of times. 60 km in 5 h, walking 6 km/h and cycling 18 km/h: average 12 km/h, time ratio 1 : 1, so 2.5 h walking = 15 km.
  • Marks, ages, salaries of two groups: the ratio gives the ratio of group sizes.

concepts.title: Alligation with a selling price and gain
concepts.body:
Alligation needs the cost price of the mixture. If the mixture is sold at a gain, first find its cost price.

CP of mixture = SP × 100/(100 + gain%).

Example: sugar at ₹30 and ₹45 per kg, mixture sold at ₹44 at 10% gain. CP = 44 × 100/110 = ₹40. Ratio = (45 − 40) : (40 − 30) = 1 : 2.

If the mixture is sold at a loss, CP = SP × 100/(100 − loss%).

concepts.title: Adding water or one ingredient
concepts.body:
When only water is added, the amount of the other ingredient stays the same. Build the equation on that fixed amount.

  • 40 L solution with 75% milk: milk = 30 L. To make milk 60%, total must be 30/0.6 = 50 L, so add 10 L water.
  • Water to add to dilute from c₁% to c₂%: V(c₁ − c₂)/c₂.
  • Pure ingredient to add to raise it from c₁% to c₂%: V(c₂ − c₁)/(100 − c₂). 80 L with 60% milk to 80% milk: 80 × 20/20 = 80 L of milk.
  • With ratios: 60 L of milk : water = 2 : 1 has 40 L milk. For 1 : 2, water must be 80 L, so add 60 L water.

concepts.title: Mixing two mixtures
concepts.body:
Change each mixture into the fraction of one ingredient, then add.

Example: vessels with milk : water 3 : 1 and 5 : 3, equal amounts mixed. Milk = 3/4 + 5/8 = 11/8, water = 1/4 + 3/8 = 5/8. Ratio = 11 : 5.

Tip: make both totals equal first. 3 : 1 = 6 : 2 (total 8) and 5 : 3 (total 8). Equal amounts give 11 : 5 directly.

To find the mixing ratio, use alligation on the fractions. Milk fraction 4/9 and 2/3, target 1/2: A : B = (2/3 − 1/2) : (1/2 − 4/9) = 3/18 : 1/18 = 3 : 1.

When containers are part full of water and topped up with milk, write each as a fraction of milk and water of the same volume and add.

concepts.title: Repeated removal and replacement
concepts.body:
A vessel holds V litres of pure liquid. x litres are taken out and replaced with water, n times. Then

Liquid left = V × (1 − x/V)ⁿ

Example: 80 L milk, 8 L replaced twice. Milk = 80 × (9/10)² = 64.8 L.

  • The formula works for any one ingredient: multiply its starting amount by (1 − x/V) each time.
  • Ratio left : original = (1 − x/V)ⁿ.
  • Part to draw off once: syrup is 11/16 of a vessel; to make it half, (11/16)(1 − f) = 1/2, so f = 3/11 of the mixture must be replaced by water.

concepts.title: Remove, then add different amounts
concepts.body:
When the amount added is different from the amount removed, the formula does not apply. Track each ingredient.

  1. Find each ingredient in the vessel.
  2. Removing mixture removes each ingredient in the same ratio as the mixture.
  3. Add the new quantities to the right ingredients.

Example: 60 L with milk : water 7 : 5 has 35 L milk and 25 L water. Remove 12 L (one fifth): 28 L milk, 20 L water. Add 8 L milk: 36 : 20 = 9 : 5.

concepts.title: Alloys and three ingredients
concepts.body:
Alloys are mixtures of metals and work the same way. Make the totals of both alloys equal, then add the parts.

Alloy P has aluminium : copper = 5 : 11 (total 16) and Q has 3 : 5 = 6 : 10 (total 16). Mixed 1 : 1: 11 : 21.

With three or more ingredients, list each ingredient’s fraction in each vessel and add ingredient by ingredient. Alligation works only between two kinds at a time.

varieties.name: Alligation of two prices or strengths
varieties.how: Write cheaper, dearer and mean. Ratio = (dearer − mean) : (mean − cheaper). Use the ratio to split the quantity. For the mean price, use the weighted average.

example.q: In what ratio must tea at ₹120 per kg be mixed with tea at ₹180 per kg so that the mixture costs ₹140 per kg?

varieties.name: Alligation with profit, interest or speed
varieties.how: Turn the data into a plain average first (CP of mixture from SP and gain, or average rate, or average speed), then apply alligation. For speeds the ratio is of times.

example.q: Sugar at ₹30 per kg is mixed with sugar at ₹45 per kg. Selling the mixture at ₹44 per kg gives a 10% gain. Find the mixing ratio.

varieties.name: Adding water or one ingredient
varieties.how: Find the amount of the ingredient that does not change. Use it to get the new total, then subtract the old total.

example.q: 40 litres of a milk solution has 75% milk. How much water must be added to make milk 60% of the solution?
steps: Milk = 75% of 40 = 30 L; it does not change.

varieties.name: Mixing two mixtures
varieties.how: Write the fraction of each ingredient in each vessel, multiply by the amount taken and add. To find the mixing ratio, use alligation on the fractions.

example.q: Vessel A has milk and water in the ratio 5 : 3 and vessel B in the ratio 3 : 1. If 2 parts of A are mixed with 3 parts of B, find the ratio of milk to water.

varieties.name: Removal and replacement
varieties.how: Liquid left = V × (1 − x/V)ⁿ, where V is the total, x the amount taken out each time, and n the number of times.

example.q: A container has 50 litres of milk. 10 litres are taken out and replaced with water. This is done 3 times in all. How much milk is left?

varieties.name: Remove some mixture, then add different amounts
varieties.how: Find each ingredient. Removing mixture takes away each ingredient in its ratio. Then add the new amounts to the right ingredients.

example.q: A 60-litre mixture has milk and water in the ratio 7 : 5. 12 litres of the mixture is removed and 8 litres of milk is added. Find the new ratio of milk to water.
steps: Removing 12 L (one fifth) leaves 28 L milk and 20 L water.

tips: Alligation gives a ratio of quantities. Check what the question asks: one quantity, total, or ratio.
Water has price ₹0 and 0% milk. Pure milk is 100% milk.
When only water is added, the milk does not change. Build the answer on the fixed part.
For mixing two ratios, make the totals of both ratios equal before adding.
For repeated replacement, multiply by (1 − x/V) once per operation.
If a mixture is sold at a gain, convert SP to CP before using alligation.
traps: Alligation with a selling price: using SP instead of the CP of the mixture gives a wrong ratio.
Average speed with alligation gives the ratio of times, not distances.
The replacement formula works only when the amount put back equals the amount taken out.
In alligation the difference goes to the opposite side: cheaper gets (dearer − mean).
“Ratio 2 : 1 of milk and water” in 60 L means 40 L milk; do not take 2 L and 1 L.

questions.q: Rice at ₹ 20 per kg is mixed with rice at ₹ 25 per kg to get a mixture worth ₹ 22 per kg. In what ratio are they mixed?
A 60-litre mixture contains milk and water in the ratio 2 : 1. How much water must be added to make the ratio 1 : 2?
questions.solution:
Milk = 40 L, water = 20 L.
For milk : water = 1 : 2, water must be 80 L.
Water to add = 80 − 20 = 60 L.

questions.q: A vessel contains 80 litres of pure milk. 8 litres are taken out and replaced with water. This is done once more. How much milk is now in the vessel?
In what ratio must water be mixed with milk costing ₹ 60 per litre to get a mixture worth ₹ 50 per litre?
Two vessels contain milk and water in the ratios 3 : 1 and 5 : 3. If equal quantities from both vessels are mixed, what is the ratio of milk to water in the new mixture?
questions.solution:
Milk fraction: 3/4 in the first, 5/8 in the second.
Take 8 L of each: milk = 6 + 5 = 11, water = 2 + 3 = 5.
Ratio = 11 : 5.

questions.q: A merchant has 1000 kg of sugar. He sells a part at 8% profit and the rest at 18% profit, gaining 14% overall. How much sugar did he sell at 18% profit?
